# Copy is the default

In C++, assignment and parameter passing COPY the whole object. When you write b = a between two std::vectors, the program allocates new memory and duplicates every element; from then on, a and b live separate lives. This sounds obvious until you arrive from Java, Python, or JavaScript, where the same line copies only a reference and the two names start pointing at the SAME object.

This choice defines the language. The good side is local reasoning: if nobody else holds a reference to your vector, nobody modifies it behind your back. No surprise aliasing, no defensive copying like in Java. The expensive side: copying a vector with a million strings means allocating a new block for the vector and a new block PER STRING, and that can happen on an innocent-looking line.

The trail's goal starts here: knowing WHEN a copy happens, how much it costs, and how to say explicitly that you do not want to pay for it. References, move, and containers, everything ahead, is a variation on this theme.

[["Language","What b = a does with an object","Consequence"],["C++","Copies the whole value","Two independent objects"],["Java","Copies the reference","Two names for the same object"],["Python","Copies the reference","Mutation shows up under both names"],["JavaScript","Copies the reference","Same shared object"]]
In C++, assignment copies. This single sentence explains half the language's hidden costs and all the aliasing surprises you will NOT have.

## Where copying truly costs

Not every copy is a problem. Copying an int, a double, or a small two-field struct costs the same as copying a pointer; the compiler resolves it in registers and the discussion ends. The cost appears when the object OWNS heap memory: vector, string, map. Copying one of those means allocating again and walking the contents, and allocation is among the most expensive operations an ordinary program does.

The classic spots where expensive copies hide: a by-value parameter of a heavy type, a return stored in a new variable unnecessarily, a push_back of an object still going to be used, a loop copying the element on every iteration because the author forgot the &.

The professional posture is not fearing the copy, it is seeing it. In code review, the question "does this line copy?" always has an exact answer: yes or no, defined by the language. Whoever masters that answer writes fast C++ with no tricks at all, just choosing signatures well.

# The signature that documents intent

A reference is a second name for the same object: no copy, no pointer syntax, no possibility of being null. Combined with const, it becomes the central API design tool in C++. A const T& parameter says "I read your object, I do not copy it and do not modify it"; a T& says "I WILL MODIFY your object"; a T by value says "I want my own copy, do whatever you want with yours".

The same holds inside classes: a method marked const promises not to alter the object's observable state. And the promise is enforced: inside a const method, any attempt to touch a member is a compilation error; on an object accessed through a const reference, only const methods may be called.

This is what the community calls const-correctness: the habit of marking everything that does not change. It is not style, it is information. Whoever reads the signature knows the contract without opening the implementation, and the compiler polices the contract on every build.

[["Signature","What it communicates to the caller"],["void f(T x)","I want an own copy; your object stays intact"],["void f(const T& x)","I only read; no copy, no change"],["void f(T& x)","I will modify YOUR object"],["double saldo() const","Querying does not alter the object's state"]]
const is not decoration: it is the part of the signature saying what the function does NOT do. An API without const forces the reader to open the implementation to discover the contract.

## The practical passing rules

To decide how to receive a parameter, the modern C++ criterion fits in three lines. Cheap-to-copy type (int, double, pointer, string_view, small structs): pass BY VALUE; the copy costs a register and a reference would only add indirection. Heavy type you only read (string, vector, domain objects): pass by const T&. Need to modify the caller's object: T&, and the function's name should make that scream.

Mark const also on methods, on local variables that do not change, and on read-only returns by reference. Every extra const narrows what the reader must consider: a function receiving only const& cannot be the culprit for the mutation you are hunting in the debugger.

There is a valuable side effect: const-correctness prepares the ground for optimization and concurrency. Objects that are only read can be shared between threads without locks. The compiler does not use const alone to optimize much, but YOUR reasoning does, and that is what avoids the expensive bugs.

All methods, generating an automatic temporary copy
Any method, as long as it is within the same file

# The role left for the pointer

Modern C++ did not abolish the raw pointer; it abolished the raw pointer as OWNER. The distinction is everything. A T* in modern code means one thing only: "I can see this object, it belongs to someone else, and it may not even exist". It is the non-owning observer, and nullptr is precisely the value representing absence.

Compare with the reference: T& cannot be null and cannot be repointed, so it communicates MANDATORY presence. The API criterion comes free: a mandatory parameter becomes a reference; an optional parameter becomes a pointer (or std::optional, which you will meet in the errors module). Whoever reads the signature knows whether to check for null.

What truly died was the hand-written new and delete pair in application code. Manual ownership demands EVERY exit path of the function remember the delete: every early return, every exception. One forgetfulness is enough to leak. Module 2 shows how RAII and smart pointers eliminate this entire bug category, at no cost.

[["You need","Use","Why"],["Read without copying, always present","const T&","Non-null by construction"],["Modify, always present","T&","No null check on the path"],["Observe, may be missing","T*","nullptr represents absence"],["Own a resource","unique_ptr or value","Automatic release, no delete"]]
A raw pointer in modern C++ says only: I can see this object. The moment it says 'this object is mine and I delete it', the code is already wrong.

## How to recognize legitimate uses

In well-kept 2026 code, the raw pointer appears in three honest places. First: optional observation parameters and returns, like the Logger* in the example, where null is a normal state. Second: the interior of data structures and low-level iteration, where it is an encapsulated implementation detail. Third: boundaries with C APIs, which only speak pointer.

Outside that, be suspicious. A loose new in the middle of a function is a sign of a failed review; a delete then, almost certainly a bug on some path. A class member of type T* as owner, with a hand-written delete in the destructor, is exactly the legacy pattern the final project of this trail will modernize.

The rule summarizing the lesson: ownership NEVER in a raw pointer; optional observation ALWAYS can be. With it in mind, reading a signature becomes reading a contract: who owns, who borrows, what may be missing. That is half the work of understanding any C++ API.

# Does it have a name, or is it a temporary?

Every expression in C++ has, besides a type, a VALUE CATEGORY. The intuition solving most cases: an lvalue is what has a name and a stable address, and keeps existing after the line; an rvalue is the temporary, born in an expression and dying at its end. The variable x is an lvalue; x + 1 is an rvalue; std::string("tmp") is an rvalue; the literal 42 is an rvalue.

Why does the language bother distinguishing? Because temporaries are an OPPORTUNITY. An object that will die at the end of the expression does not need to be copied with care: its resources can be stolen without anyone noticing. For that to work, the compiler must know for certain when something is a temporary, and the value category is exactly that information.

C++11 gave a reference type for this: T&& is the rvalue reference, which only binds to temporaries. The old const T& is generous: it binds to lvalues and rvalues. This pair is the mechanical basis of move semantics, the central subject of module 3.

[["Expression","Category","Why"],["x","lvalue","Has a name and a stable address"],["x + 1","rvalue","Nameless temporary"],["std::string(\"tmp\")","rvalue","Born and dies in the expression"],["std::move(x)","rvalue (xvalue)","Cast treating x as a temporary"],["s inside g(std::string&& s)","lvalue","The parameter has a name and an address"]]
The question separating the categories is simple: does this have a name and keep existing after the line? It has a name, it is an lvalue. It is an anonymous temporary, it is an rvalue.

## The trap that trips everyone

Inside void g(std::string&& s), what is the category of s? The TYPE of s is rvalue reference, but s HAS A NAME, so the expression s is an lvalue. It looks like pedantry and it is the key to everything: if you pass s onward to another function, it will be treated as an lvalue and be COPIED, not moved. To forward the temporary as a temporary, you must write std::move(s) again. Keep the sentence: a named rvalue reference is an lvalue.

The standard's complete picture has five categories (the useful novelty is the xvalue, the "expiring value" std::move produces), but the practical split between "has identity and remains" and "can be plundered" covers the daily work of whoever writes application code.

What you take from this lesson: const T& accepts everything and promises only to read; T&& captures temporaries and opens the door to resource stealing; and a named T&& becomes an lvalue again. With these three facts, the move semantics module stops being magic and becomes mechanics.

# When auto clarifies and when it hides

auto asks the compiler to deduce the type from the expression. It was born to kill noise: nobody needs to type std::map<std::string, std::vector<int>>::const_iterator when the line below makes obvious what the variable is. With structured bindings, a loop over a map becomes for (const auto& [chave, valor] : mapa), which reads like the intent.

The first safety rule: auto COPIES. In auto x = expr, x is a new object, deduced WITHOUT reference and without const. If the expression returns a reference to something expensive, plain auto silently pays a copy. Want to reference, write auto&; want only to read, const auto&. Choosing among these three forms is exactly the parameter-passing decision you already trained.

The second rule: auto hides the type from the READER, not from the compiler. In an expression whose type is the relevant information (arithmetic with sizes and indices, public API boundaries), writing the type in full is kindness to whoever reviews.

[["Form","What it does","When to use"],["auto x = expr","Deduces and COPIES the value","Type obvious from context"],["auto& x = expr","Mutable reference","Modifying the original in the loop"],["const auto& x","Read-only reference","Reading expensive elements without copying"],["explicit type","Documents the intent","API boundary; the type matters"]]
auto removes the noise, not the responsibility: you still need to know the type. The difference is that now the compiler checks it, not the reader.

## The proxy trap

Some types lie to auto. The classic case is std::vector<bool>: due to a historical space optimization, operator[] does not return a bool, it returns a proxy object REFERENCING one bit inside the vector. With bool b = flags[0], the proxy converts and you receive a true bool. With auto p = flags[0], p STORES THE PROXY, which stays tied to the vector: if flags is reallocated or destroyed, using p is undefined behavior.

The same pattern appears in linear algebra libraries with expression templates, where adding matrices returns an expression object, not a matrix. The defense is simple: when the expression may return a proxy, name the desired type on the left side and force the conversion.

Closing the module is the posture summary: auto by default where the type is obvious, auto& and const auto& conscious of copying, explicit type where the reader needs it, and trained suspicion of the rare proxy types. Deduction is comfort, and good comfort is the kind that hides no cost.

# The resource tied to the scope

RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) is C++'s most important idea, and the terrible name hides a simple mechanism: the CONSTRUCTOR acquires the resource, the DESTRUCTOR releases it, and the compiler guarantees the destructor runs when the object leaves scope. Resource here is anything needing return: memory, an open file, a locked mutex, a network connection, a database transaction.

The practical consequence: you do not write release code. There is no forgotten close, forgotten unlock, forgotten free, because release is not a line someone must remember; it is a grammatical consequence of the scope's end. The block ends, the destructors run, in the reverse order of construction.

And the detail separating C++ from garbage-collected languages: the moment is DETERMINISTIC. The file closes exactly there, the mutex unlocks exactly there, not "when the collector passes". For scarce resources like locks and connections, that "exactly there" is the difference between a predictable system and a system that chokes.

[["Resource","RAII class","What the destructor does"],["Dynamic memory","vector, string, unique_ptr","Frees the block"],["File","ifstream, ofstream","Closes the descriptor"],["Mutex","lock_guard, scoped_lock","Unlocks"],["Connection or transaction","Your wrapper","Ends or rolls back"]]
In C++ you do not write 'release this': you write 'this lives in this scope'. Release becomes a consequence of grammar, including when an exception crosses the function.

## Exception safety for free

The decisive argument for RAII is the error path. When an exception is thrown, stack unwinding destroys, one by one, every local object already constructed between the throw and the catch. If every resource lives inside an RAII object, the error path cleans up EVERYTHING by itself, in the right order, without a line written by you. In the lesson's example, the throw happens with the mutex locked; still nobody deadlocks, because the lock_guard unlocks during unwinding.

Compare with languages needing try/finally or with: there cleanup is opt-in, and every usage point must remember the pattern. In C++ cleanup is opt-out: it happens unless you sabotage it.

The discipline that stays: EVERY resource lives inside an object whose destructor returns it. If you are holding a resource in a raw variable and releasing by hand, stop and wrap. The next lessons present the standard library's ready wrappers for the most common case of all, memory.

# The zero-cost unique owner

std::unique_ptr<T> is RAII applied to memory with the simplest possible rule: ONE owner per object. The unique_ptr holds the pointer, its destructor calls delete, and copying is forbidden at compile time, because copying would create two owners. What exists is MOVING: ownership is transferred, the old owner is left null, and there continues to be exactly one responsible party.

The cost is the argument that disarms skeptics: none. A unique_ptr with the default deleter is the size of a raw pointer and generates the same machine code as correctly written manual new/delete. There is no counter, no synchronization, no hidden overhead. You trade an entire class of bugs (leak, double free, forgotten delete) for nothing.

Always create with std::make_unique<T>(args): the allocation and the owner's construction happen in a single expression, with no new appearing in your code. In review, the rule is binary: visible new outside a factory is a smell; make_unique is the standard.

[["Signature","Ownership contract"],["unique_ptr<T> f()","The function creates and DELIVERS the owner to the caller"],["void f(unique_ptr<T> p)","The function TAKES ownership of the object"],["void f(const T& x)","Only reads; ownership remains with the caller"],["T* f()","Returns an observer; nobody transfers ownership"]]
unique_ptr is the delete you do not write: the same size as a pointer, the same speed, and ownership documented in the type system.

## unique_ptr designing APIs

unique_ptr's silent gain is what it does for signatures. A factory returning std::unique_ptr<Relatorio> says, with no comment at all: I created it, the owner is now you. A function receiving unique_ptr BY VALUE says: hand me ownership; the caller must write std::move at the call site, and that word on screen is the visual warning that they gave the object up.

To merely use the object, the function should NOT receive unique_ptr: it receives const T& or T&. Passing a smart pointer to whoever only reads couples the function to the caller's ownership strategy and prevents calling it with stack objects. Whoever only reads does not need to know who the owner is.

Complete the picture with two utilities: p.get() returns the raw pointer to interoperate with observing APIs, and p.reset() releases early or swaps the object. And when the object is optional inside a class, a null unique_ptr member represents absence with guaranteed automatic release.

# Shared ownership has a price

std::shared_ptr<T> implements SHARED ownership: every copy increments a counter, every destruction decrements it, and the last owner out turns off the lights, deleting the object. Next to the object lives a control block with the counter, and there lies the cost: the counter is ATOMIC, because owners may live on different threads. Every shared_ptr copy is an atomic read-modify-write operation, which forces synchronization between cores and invalidates cache lines. Copied inside a hot loop, shared_ptr becomes a measurable bottleneck.

Prefer std::make_shared<T>(args) when constructing: object and control block are born in a single neighboring allocation, better for allocator and cache, instead of two separate allocations.

And the design rule preventing abuse: shared_ptr is for when ownership is GENUINELY shared, with no owner whose life is guaranteed longer. If a natural owner exists, unique_ptr on it and references for the rest solve it cheaper and clearer.

[["Aspect","shared_ptr","weak_ptr"],["Counts in the ownership counter","Yes, atomically","No; observes the block"],["Keeps the object alive","Yes","No"],["How to access","Directly, like a pointer","lock() returns shared or empty"],["Role in a cycle","Creates the leak","Breaks the leak"]]
When everyone is an owner, nobody is: shared_ptr scattered across the codebase is usually the signature of a design that never decided who is in charge of whom.

## Cycles, and how weak_ptr breaks them

Reference counting has a famous blind spot: the CYCLE. If Pai holds a shared_ptr to Filho and Filho holds a shared_ptr to Pai, the two counters never reach zero, even when the rest of the program forgot both. No destructor runs; memory leaks silently. Garbage collectors detect cycles; reference counting does not.

The solution is deciding the DIRECTION of ownership: the father owns the child (shared_ptr downward), the child merely OBSERVES the father (weak_ptr upward). weak_ptr knows the control block but does not count as an owner. To use it, call lock(): if the object still lives, you receive a temporary shared_ptr keeping it alive during use; if it already died, you receive empty and handle the absence. No dangling, no holding anyone's life hostage.

The pattern holds for any back-reference: caches pointing at entries, observers pointing at the publisher, children to parents. Ownership flows down; observation flows up.

lessons.title: The rule of zero, three, and five

blocks.value:
# When the compiler suffices

The compiler knows how to generate six special functions for your class: default constructor, destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor, and move assignment. The RULE OF ZERO says: if all your members are already RAII types (string, vector, unique_ptr), write NONE of them. The generated versions copy member by member, move member by member, and destroy member by member, and that is exactly the correct behavior. A well-designed domain class has zero special functions and zero management bugs.

The problem starts when the class manages a RAW resource: a new[] pointer, a system file handle, a socket. The generated destructor cannot release that, so you write a destructor. And here enters the RULE OF THREE, inherited from C++98: whoever writes the destructor must also write the copy (constructor and assignment), because the generated versions would copy the POINTER, not the resource, and two destructors would release the same block.

[["Class situation","Rule","What to write"],["Only RAII members","Zero","Nothing; the compiler generates it all right"],["Manages a raw resource","Five","Destructor, copy, and move (or =delete)"],["Polymorphic base","Zero + virtual","Virtual destructor =default"],["Copy makes no sense","Explicit","Copy =delete; move if it makes sense"]]
If you wrote a destructor, the compiler no longer knows how to copy or move your class correctly. The rule of five is the full bill for that warning.

## From three to five, and the =default and =delete tools

C++11 added move to the package and three became FIVE: destructor, copy (constructor and assignment), and move (constructor and assignment). The treacherous detail: declaring a destructor or copy SUPPRESSES move generation. The class still compiles, but every std::move on it silently becomes a copy. It is the kind of performance regression no functional test catches, and the reason the rule of five is charged in review.

Two words complete the vocabulary. With =default you explicitly request the generated version (useful for a base's virtual destructor: virtual ~Base() = default). With =delete you forbid the operation: a class that must not be copied declares the copy as deleted and the error appears at the COMPILATION of whoever tries, not in production.

# The signature tells who owns

Put the module's pieces together and the result is a communication system: in modern C++, the SIGNATURE declares the ownership relationship between caller and callee. T by value: I want my own copy (or I will consume the data). const T&: I only read, the owner is you. T&: I modify yours, the owner remains you. T*: I observe, it may not exist. unique_ptr<T> by value: transfer ownership to me. shared_ptr<T>: we will own it together, with a counter. weak_ptr<T>: I want to be able to ask whether it still exists.

Read this way, an API becomes a responsibility map. You glance at std::unique_ptr<Conexao> abrir(Config) and know the function manufactures and delivers; at void enviar(const Pacote&) and know nobody changes or retains anything; at Estatisticas* metricas() and know the return is borrowed and may be missing.

# The waste old C++ accepted

Take the most common operation of a real program: assembling a collection and returning it. In C++98, every step of this routine could fire a complete copy. A string temporary created in a concatenation was COPIED to the destination and thrown away. A push_back of a temporary copied the object into the vector and destroyed the original an instant later. And when the vector outgrew its capacity, all elements were copied to the new block, one by one.

Notice the specific absurdity of the case: the copy's source was an object ABOUT TO DIE. We copied a million bytes from a buffer that would be released on the next line, when it would suffice to... keep the buffer. The dying object needed no expensive farewell; it needed to be plundered.

Programmers of the era worked around it with tricks: passing the destination by reference to fill it, clever swap functions, manual reference counting. C++11 turned the trick into a language feature: MOVE, the official capacity to transfer the resources of an object on its way out.

## What move promises

The central idea fits in one sentence: when the SOURCE is a temporary, instead of duplicating its resources, the destination TAKES them. For a vector, that means three pointers changing hands (begin, end, capacity) instead of a new allocation and a copy traversal; for a string, the whole buffer changes owners in constant time. The cost plummets from O(n) with allocation to O(1) without allocation.

And the safety comes from module 1's lvalue and rvalue lesson: the compiler KNOWS when an expression is a temporary. The overload taking T&& is only chosen for rvalues, so resource stealing only happens when nobody else will look at the source. No legitimate copy changes behavior; only the waste disappears.

In this module you will see the four pieces of the mechanics: what std::move really is (lesson 2), how to write move constructor and assignment with noexcept (lesson 3), what the compiler already elides without you asking (lesson 4), and the places where the move does NOT happen and the copy returns in silence (lesson 5).

# The worst-named cast in the language

std::move moves nothing. It is a CAST: it converts the expression to an rvalue (technically an xvalue), and nothing more. Not one byte moves when you write std::move(x). What the conversion does is change WHICH overload will be chosen next: with the expression marked as an rvalue, the type's move constructor (or move assignment) starts winning the overload resolution dispute. The one who moves is the CONSTRUCTOR; std::move only opens the door.

The correct reading of auto b = std::move(a) is: "I declare that I no longer care about a's value; type, do whatever is cheapest". If the type has move, a's resources are stolen. If it does not, the code COMPILES JUST THE SAME and makes a copy. That is the silent trap: std::move is a request, not a guarantee, and lesson 5 shows the cases where the request is denied.

Internally it is just static_cast<T&&>(x). A name like as_rvalue would have spared a decade of confusion.

## The valid-but-unspecified state

What is left in the source after the move? The standard answers with bureaucratic precision: a VALID, YET UNSPECIFIED state. Valid means the class's invariants still stand: you may destroy it, reassign it, call methods without preconditions (size, clear, empty). Unspecified means the VALUE is not promised: the moved string usually ends up empty in practice (with SSO it may even keep the characters), but writing code depending on that is a bug waiting for a new compiler.

The usage discipline is short: after moving, either the object dies, or it receives a new value before any read. std::unique_ptr is the pleasant exception, with a stronger guarantee: moved, it becomes null, and testing against nullptr is legitimate.

# Writing the theft by hand

When the class follows the rule of zero, move comes for free. But you need to know how to write it, both for the inevitable raw-resource cases and to READ what the compiler generates. The move constructor's recipe has three steps: STEAL the source's pointers and values (shallow copy, cheap), ZERO the source so its destructor does not release what is now yours, and nothing else. No allocation, no walking data: just a change of ownership.

Move assignment adds two cares: release the destination's CURRENT resource before stealing (otherwise it leaks) and guard against self-move, because a = std::move(a), however absurd, must not corrupt the object.

And the word that is not optional: NOEXCEPT. A move that does not allocate has no reason to throw, and declaring it changes the standard library's behavior, as the next block shows. Every move constructor and assignment you write in this trail carries noexcept, and your reviewer will charge the same.

## Why vector demands noexcept

When a vector reallocates, it must transport the elements to the new block while maintaining the STRONG guarantee: if something throws midway, the original vector remains intact. With copy, the guarantee is easy: if copy number 700 thousand throws, the old block stays complete; the new one is thrown away. With move, no: the first 700 thousand elements were already PLUNDERED from the old block, and there is no way back without moving again (and the move back could throw too).

The library's way out is contractual: vector uses std::move_if_noexcept. If your type's move is noexcept, it moves, fast. If it is not, it COPIES everything, to preserve the guarantee. The practical consequence is brutal: forgetting noexcept breaks nothing visibly, it just makes every reallocation pay a full copy.

# The compiler elides before you optimize

Before applying move everywhere, learn what the compiler already does ALONE. RVO (Return Value Optimization) is copy elision on return: instead of constructing the object inside the function and transporting it out, the compiler constructs the object DIRECTLY in the caller's slot. No copy, no move: both ends use the same address from the start.

Since C++17, this stopped being an optional optimization in an important case: returning a prvalue (return std::vector<int>(1000000)) has elision GUARANTEED by language rule. It is not the optimizer being kind; it is the standard demanding it. The type does not even need a copy or move constructor in that case.

When you return a NAMED local variable (build v, fill it, return v), NRVO (Named RVO) enters: permitted and practiced by compilers in the vast majority of cases, but not guaranteed. And the fallback, if NRVO does not apply, is already good: a local variable in a return is automatically treated as an rvalue, so a MOVE comes out, never an expensive copy.

## Return by value, without fear

The consequence of RVO, NRVO, and move together is a liberating API rule: RETURN BY VALUE. The function manufacturing a vector returns the vector; the one assembling a string returns the string. The old reflex of receiving a T& output to "avoid the return copy" has lost its technical reason to exist, and costs dearly in readability: an output parameter does not make clear what the function produces, prevents composing calls, and forces the caller to pre-construct an empty object.

For NRVO to work in your favor, help the compiler: return ONE local variable (not choosing between two in different branches), of the same type as the return, without wrapping it in creative conditionals. Functions that create and return in a direct flow gain elision almost always.

And the mental test for review stays: if you see a std::move in a return of a local variable, or an output parameter in a new function, the question is "which copy is this trying to avoid?". In 2026, the answer is almost always: one that no longer existed.

# The places where the copy returns in silence

Move has a treacherous property: when it does NOT happen, the program stays correct, only slower. No warning by default, no failing test. This lesson is the map of the holes.

The first and most common: CONST KILLS MOVE. std::move on a const variable produces a const T&&, which does not match the move constructor (it asks for T&& without const). Overload resolution politely falls to the copy, which accepts const T&. A const std::string local, moved in a return or into a member, copies. The lesson is not abandoning const, it is knowing that an object declared const is an object that will be copied, and deciding with that information.

The second: PARAMETERS RECEIVED BY VALUE need std::move when storing. Inside Perfil(std::string nome), nome is an lvalue (it has a name!); nome_(nome) copies. The correct idiom is nome_(std::move(nome)): the parameter is already your private copy, move it to its final destination without paying again.

# The compiler writes the code

A template is not a function: it is a MOLD for a function. When you write template <typename T> and use menor(3, 7), the compiler INSTANTIATES the mold with T = int, generating a concrete function menor<int> as if you had typed it. Use it with double and another function is born; with std::string, one more. This process is called monomorphization: every type used gets its own machine code, specialized and optimizable, with no runtime indirection at all.

Compare with inheritance polymorphism: a virtual function is ONE function, chosen at runtime via vtable, paying the indirection on every call. The template resolves everything at compilation, free at runtime, at the cost of a bigger binary (one copy per type) and slower compilation.

And the requirement on T is STRUCTURAL, not nominal: menor demands only that T have operator<. It does not matter from whom T inherits, it matters what T can do. It is duck typing, except verified at compile time: if the type lacks the operation, the program is not even born.

That is why a std::vector of a type without operator== works perfectly, until the day someone calls v1 == v2 and the error appears: the comparison is only demanded when the comparison is instantiated.

Second: the deep verification of the body happens AT INSTANTIATION. The compiler checks the mold's syntax when reading it, but only checks whether T can take the operations when a concrete T arrives. # The compilation model explained

The rule every beginner trips on: template definitions live in the HEADER. The reason is C++'s compilation model. Each .cpp file is a translation unit compiled in isolation; to instantiate menor<int>, the compiler needs to SEE the mold's complete body at that moment. If the body hides in another .cpp, the current unit can only note "someone owes me menor<int>", and since no unit generates that instance, the LINKER breaks with the classic undefined reference.

That is why the practice's standard is direct: whole template in the .hpp, body next to the declaration. Every .cpp including the header instantiates what it uses; the linker, at the end, finds the duplicate instances across units and discards the extra copies, keeping one of each.

The price is not correctness, it is BUILD: the same menor<int> is compiled in every unit using it, and projects with heavy templates in widely included headers feel it in minutes of recompilation. Mitigations exist and are the subject of the final block.

[["Strategy","What it does","Effect on the build"],["Everything in the header","Each unit instantiates what it uses","Simple; recompiles a lot"],["extern template","Instantiates once in a .cpp","Less repeated work"],["Modules (C++20)","Interface compiled once","Adoption still uneven in 2026"]]
The linker accepts seeing the same template instance in ten units: it discards nine. What it does not forgive is finding none.

## Living with the build cost

The weapons against slow builds have different reach. Explicit instantiation with extern template serves when few instances dominate: you declare "do not instantiate here" in the using units and materialize the instance a single time in a dedicated .cpp. Libraries do this for common types (libstdc++ itself does it with std::string, which is basically basic_string<char> instantiated).

C++20 MODULES attack the root: the interface is compiled once into a binary format and imported, instead of being textually reprocessed on every inclusion. In 2026, support in the three major compilers exists and the std is already importable as a module in C++23, but the ecosystem migration (build systems, older libraries) remains gradual; new projects can adopt, legacies advance slowly.

Meanwhile, the hygienes hold: lean template headers, minimal includes in them, and heavy types explicitly instantiated. And the always-criterion: measure the build before moving code around; the real slowness almost always has three or four concentrated culprits.

# Two ways to customize per type

Sooner or later the generic needs exceptions: serializing bool differently from int, formatting string with quotes, treating pointer another way. C++ gives two tools, and choosing wrong generates subtle bugs.

SPECIALIZATION replaces the template's body for a specific type: template <> struct Serial<bool> rewrites the bool version entirely. Classes accept TOTAL specialization (one exact type) and PARTIAL specialization (a family: Serial<std::vector<T>> for any T). It is the right tool for customizing CLASSES, where overloading does not exist.

OVERLOAD is a second function with the same name, more specific: beside the generic template rotulo(const T&), you declare rotulo(const std::string&). At the call, overload resolution prefers the non-template function that matches exactly. For FUNCTIONS, that is the right tool, for the next section's reasons. And functions do not even have partial specialization: the feature simply does not exist in the language; what looks like it is always another overload.

[["Goal","Tool","Reason"],["Function with a special case","Overload","Participates in resolution; predictable"],["Class with per-type layout","Total or partial specialization","Overloading does not exist for classes"],["Family of types in a function","Another, more specific template","Function partial does not exist"],["Behavior by property","Concepts and requires (lesson 4)","Readable and verified criterion"]]
The rule of thumb avoiding a whole class of surprises: specialize CLASSES, overload FUNCTIONS. When in doubt, it is an overload.

## Why overload wins for functions

Total function specialization EXISTS (template <> std::string rotulo<bool>...), and that is exactly why the rule must be said: it has surprising behavior. Specializations do NOT participate in overload resolution. The compiler first chooses among PRIMARY functions and templates; only after electing a template does it check whether a specialization of it exists to use. Famous result: depending on declaration order and the set of overloads, your specialization is solemnly ignored, and which function runs changes with its position in the file.

Overloads do not have this problem: all enter the dispute together, with unique rules (the most specific wins), and the result does not depend on order across files. Hence the guidelines' dry directive: to customize a function per type, write another overload, never a template <>.

Note the operational summary: classes ask for specialization (there is no alternative); functions ask for overload (the alternative exists and bites). In the trail's next module, concepts will give functions a third path, restricting by the type's PROPERTY instead of exact type.

# Constraints that read like sentences

For twenty years, restricting a template was handicraft with enable_if and SFINAE: it worked, and it was unreadable. C++20 promoted constraint to a first-class feature: CONCEPTS. A concept is a NAMED set of requirements on types, verified at compilation, written with the requires keyword in declarative syntax.

The effect shows on both sides. In the declaration, template <std::integral T> says on the first line what the function accepts; the contract leaves the comment and enters the code. In the error, the message changes nature: instead of two hundred lines of failed substitution in the library's guts, the compiler says "constraint not satisfied" and points at WHICH requirement your type fails. It is the difference between a diagnosis and a context dump.

In 2026, C++20 is the common base of new projects, and concepts are the standard for generic code other people will use. The library already carries a ready vocabulary in <concepts> (integral, floating_point, convertible_to, same_as) and the range concepts (sortable, range, input_iterator).

## requires from the inside, without overdoing it

The expression requires(const T& t) { ... } lists what must COMPILE for the type to pass: valid expressions ({ t.nome() }), compatible return types (-> std::convertible_to<...>), existing nested types (typename T::value_type). Important: the check is syntactic and about types, done entirely at compilation; nobody executes t.nome() to test. A type can satisfy the concept and still misbehave at runtime; a concept verifies FORM, not semantics.

In overload resolution, concepts also order: between two viable templates, the more specific constraint wins, which lets you write the general case and the refined case without tricks.

And the maturity advice: constrain what the function REALLY demands, not everything the type could have. A bloated concept is as bad as a missing one: it refuses legitimate types and couples the interface to details. Start with the library's concepts; write your own when the domain asks for its own vocabulary, and give them the names your team would use in a conversation.

# Technique against the wall of text

Template errors scare by VOLUME, not by difficulty. A one-character slip can dump three hundred lines, but the useful information occupies three. The technique is knowing which three.

Rule one: read the FIRST error, ignore the rest. The second error onward is usually an echo of the first; fix the first, recompile, and reassess. Rule two: look for the chain of "required from here" and follow it to the line pointing at YOUR file. The error bursts deep, inside the library, but it was your usage that fired it; your code's line is the fix point. Rule three: in the "no matching function" block, the rejected candidates come with the reason for each rejection; read the reasons, not the giant names.

And learn to DISCARD noise: types appear with all default parameters expanded (std::vector<int, std::allocator<int>>, basic_string with three arguments). Mentally erase the allocators and char_traits; what remains is readable.

# Size, capacity, and the contiguous block

std::vector is a CONTIGUOUS heap block plus three pointers: begin, end of content, and end of block. From that come the two numbers you must distinguish: size() is how many elements exist; capacity() is how many fit before needing a new block. While size < capacity, a push_back costs constructing one element at the end, and nothing more.

When capacity runs out, REALLOCATION happens: a bigger block is allocated (geometric growth, typically 1.5x to 2x), the elements are transported (moved, if the move is noexcept, as you saw in module 3), and the old block is released. It is an expensive event, but rare by construction: with geometric growth, inserting n elements costs O(n) amortized in total, and that is what "push_back is amortized O(1)" means.

The immediate operational consequence: when you KNOW how many elements are coming, say so. v.reserve(n) makes a single early allocation and zeroes the fill's reallocations. It is the one-line optimization with the STL's best return.

[["Operation","Cost","Invalidates iterators and pointers?"],["push_back without reallocation","O(1)","No"],["push_back with reallocation","O(n) on that event","ALL"],["insert in the middle","O(n): shifts the tail","From that point on; all if reallocating"],["reserve(n)","O(n) a single time","All, once"],["operator[] and traversal","O(1) per access","No"]]
Every vector iterator carries an invisible expiration date: the next push_back may be the reallocation turning your pointer into a bomb.

## Invalidation: the classic bug

The price of the contiguous block is INVALIDATION: reallocated, every pointer, reference, and iterator to the old content becomes garbage. The classic bug has two forms. The first: keeping a pointer or reference to an element and continuing to insert; it works in tests (while capacity holds) and explodes in production the day the data grows. The second: inserting or erasing INSIDE a loop iterating the very vector, using the old iterator after the modification.

The defenses, in order of preference: do not keep pointers into a vector that still changes (keep INDICES, which survive reallocation); if the final size is known, reserve beforehand and capacity does not change during the fill; and when erasing while iterating, use erase's return (it = v.erase(it)) or C++20's std::erase_if, which encapsulates the whole pattern.

Also the symmetry warning: shrink_to_fit and erase itself do not guaranteedly return memory or cheapen anything by themselves; measuring before "optimizing" memory counts as much as for CPU.

# Tree, hash, and the cost the table does not show

std::map is a balanced binary tree (red-black in implementations): search, insertion, and removal in O(log n), keys always in ORDER, and therefore range queries (lower_bound, upper_bound) and ordered iteration come naturally. std::unordered_map is a hash table: amortized O(1) on exact-key search, no order, and occasional rehash when the load factor overflows.

But asymptotic notation hides the factor weighing most in 2026: MEMORY. Both are node-based containers: every element is a separate allocation, scattered across the heap. Searching a map of one million entries is twenty pointer hops, and every hop is a probable cache miss of hundreds of cycles. The unordered hops less, but still chases pointers to buckets.

Hence the heuristic surprising beginners: for SMALL collections (tens, a few hundreds), a vector of pairs with linear or binary search often beats BOTH, because it traverses contiguous memory the CPU's prefetcher loves.

The complexity table has no column for cache misses. It is in that invisible column that vector beats map in half of real cases.

## The choosing criterion, without ranking

The healthy decision starts from two questions. First: do you need ORDER or range queries? If yes, map (or a sorted-kept vector, if insertions are rare and reads dominate). If not, the fight is between unordered_map and vector: exact key only, large and mutable N, unordered wins; small N or an intense reading phase after assembling once, the flat vector tends to win.

Second: is this container on a HOT path? If it is, the final answer comes from no table, it comes from MEASUREMENT with real data, because the result depends on key sizes (hashing a long string costs), access distribution, and whatever else disputes the cache.

Two fine adjustments worth knowing: unordered_map accepts reserve(n) to avoid rehashing during loads (the same reflex as vector), and string keys benefit from heterogeneous lookup (find with string_view, without constructing a temporary std::string). # The string that does not go to the heap

std::string is a vector of chars with one extra trick: SSO, the small string optimization. SHORT strings live inside the object itself, in an internal buffer, with no heap allocation at all. Only when the text exceeds the limit does the string allocate. The exact limit varies by implementation (in 2026, libc++ keeps up to 22 chars inline and libstdc++ up to 15), so the portable rule is qualitative: identifiers, codes, and short names are free; long texts allocate.

The impact is large because short strings DOMINATE real programs: map keys, log fields, file names. Copying an SSO string is copying bytes on the stack, no heap; a vector<string> of short words is far more cache-friendly than "a bunch of pointers" suggests.

Two practical consequences: string benchmarks made only with shortish texts measure SSO, not the string; and moving a short string is not cheaper than copying it, because there is no pointer to steal, the bytes are copied either way.

string_view is a loan with no guarantor: cheap, direct, and it is your responsibility to ensure the text's owner stays alive while the view circulates.

## string_view and the non-owner discipline

std::string_view is a pointer-size pair: a read WINDOW into characters belonging to someone else. As an input parameter, it is the modern standard: it accepts string, literal, buffer piece, everything without allocating or copying, and substr on a view costs pointer arithmetic, not allocation.

The danger is the same as span and every reference: DANGLING. The view extends nobody's life. The two classic accidents: returning a view to a local string (it dies at the return) and storing a view as a class MEMBER while the original text is temporary or reallocates. Remember that methods like std::string::substr return a NEW temporary string; chaining .substr(...) into a call receiving a view creates exactly the temporary that dies at the expression's end.

The discipline that solves it: view as PARAMETER, freely; view as return or member, only with an explicit lifetime contract (for example, views to static literals or to a buffer the class itself owns). In doubt, promote to std::string and pay the copy with pride: a dangling bug costs more than any allocation.

# Say the operation by name

A raw loop with for, if, and break is a puzzle the reader reassembles every time. The <algorithm> plus lambda pair swaps the puzzle for a NAME: find_if finds the first satisfying; count_if counts; transform maps; sort orders by a criterion; erase_if removes. The reader reads the intent; the compiler sees monomorphized code (the lambda becomes an inline functor, without the function-pointer cost).

The lambda is the piece that unlocked this style: an anonymous function with CAPTURE of context. [limite](const Pedido& p) { return p.total > limite; } carries the limit into the predicate. Capture by value ([x]) to store a copy; by reference ([&x]) to see the original variable, with the responsibility of keeping it alive while the lambda runs.

The safety rule avoiding the classic accident: a lambda that OUTLIVES the scope (stored in a member, a callback queue, a thread) captures by VALUE. Capture by reference is for immediate use, inside the expression or the function.

## Ranges: the evolution that composes

The classic algorithms have two frictions: the repetitive begin/end pair and poor composition (filtering AND transforming asks for an intermediate vector or a hybrid loop). C++20 RANGES solve both. std::ranges::sort(pedidos) takes the whole container; and the VIEWS (filter, transform, take, drop) chain with the pipe, forming LAZY pipelines: nothing is computed until someone traverses the result, and no intermediate container is born.

The reading changes shape: data | filter | transformation, in the order you would narrate the process out loud. And since views are non-owning (windows over the original container, relatives of string_view), the same lifetime rules hold: do not let the view outlive the container, and do not modify the container while iterating the view.

The adoption criterion in 2026: ranges for read-and-transform pipelines, where they shine; classic algorithms remain perfect for point actions (sort, find) and are what you will most find in existing codebases. # vector first, the rest with a reason

After four lessons of costs, the module's synthesis is one policy: start with VECTOR, switch when the access pattern gives a nameable reason. Not because vector is "the best container", but because contiguous memory is the default 2026's machine rewards: cache exploited, prefetch working, zero allocation per element. The alternatives exist for specific access patterns, and this lesson's table is their map.

The example ending the urban legend: std::list. On paper, O(1) insertion in the middle; in practice, every node is an allocation and every advance a pointer hop, and FINDING the insertion point costs a traversal burying the advantage. In 2026, with the CPU-memory gap still growing, list loses to vector even in middle-insertion benchmarks for moderate sizes. It survives for a niche: elements that CANNOT move (external pointers to them) with insertions at already-known positions.

Criterion, not ranking: every structure has the access pattern where it wins. Your job is naming your pattern before choosing.

# The model, the cost, and who turns it off

C++'s exception model has a real elegance: the error climbs ALONE to whoever can handle it, crossing ten layers without polluting any signature, and stack unwinding destroys the local objects along the way, which makes RAII the perfect pair for throw. Rare error, handled far away, with automatic cleanup: that is the use case exceptions were designed for.

The cost is asymmetric by design. Modern implementations are "zero-cost" on the HAPPY PATH: no cycles spent while nothing is thrown, because the unwinding information sits in static tables in the binary. The THROW PATH, however, is expensive and, worse, UNPREDICTABLE: walking tables, unwinding frames, destroying objects; latency varies with stack depth and cache state.

That unpredictability explains who disables them (-fno-exceptions): games with a 16 ms per-frame budget, embedded with binaries counted in kilobytes, kernels and latency-critical systems. It is not cultural grumpiness; it is the cold path's cost not fitting the budget.

## The usage criterion that survives review

Three rules separate mature use from abuse. First: exception for EXCEPTIONAL failure, one the immediate caller cannot resolve (missing config at startup, broken invariant, out of memory). EXPECTED domain failure (user not found, invalid input, network timeout) is not exceptional: it is a result, and the next lessons show the types representing it better.

Second: throw by VALUE, catch by CONST REFERENCE (catch (const std::exception& e)). Catching by value slices the object to the base type and loses the derived type's information; catching by pointer creates ownership doubt.

Third: exceptions demand EXCEPTION-SAFE code underneath, and in C++ that means one concrete thing: every resource in RAII, no manual cleanup between the point that can throw and the end of the scope. If code mixes loose new with functions that throw, the leak is not a risk, it is a schedule. In the previous modules you built exactly the base making exceptions safe; without it, the whole model collapses.

# Absence and failure, typed in the return

EXPECTED failure deserves to live in the return type, where the compiler forces everyone to look at it. Modern C++ gives two vehicles.

std::optional<T> represents ABSENCE: the search that may not find, the field that may not exist, the parse of what may be empty. Either it has a T, or it has nothing, and "nothing" here is not an error: it is a legitimate answer. The idiomatic use tests and accesses: if (auto u = buscar(id)) { usar(*u); }.

std::expected<T, E>, from C++23, represents FAILURE WITH A REASON: either the value, or a TYPED error saying why. It answers the question optional cannot: "it did not come... but why?". The error travels as an ordinary value, no unwinding, with the predictable cost of a branch, and the signature becomes a complete contract: std::expected<Config, ErroConfig> carregar(...) lists success AND failure in the same place. In 2026, with the three major compilers supporting it, expected is the emerging standard for expected failure in new APIs.

## Chaining without a pyramid of ifs

The scale gain comes from the MONADIC operations of C++23, which both types share. and_then chains the next step that can also fail; transform applies a function to the value, if any; or_else and value_or resolve the empty case at the chain's end. A pipeline carregar().and_then(validar).transform(extrairPorta).value_or(8080) reads like the business logic, and the chain's first error short-circuits the following steps without a single nested if.

Three disciplines keep the pattern healthy. First: optional is for ABSENCE; if there is a failure reason the caller may want to distinguish, it is expected (resist the laziness of optional that swallows the why). Second: accessing with * without testing is UB with optional and with expected; the pipelines exist precisely to concentrate the test in one place. Third: the error type E should be small and enumerable (the next lesson takes care of it); expected with a giant E becomes a disguised exception with copy cost.

With these two types, expected failure leaves the comment and enters the contract. What remains for exceptions is what was always theirs: the genuinely exceptional.

# enum class and the return that shouts

Before expected existed, and still today at system boundaries and in code without exceptions, the failure vehicle is the ERROR CODE. The well-made version starts with enum class: a scoped enumeration (ErroRede::timeout, not a bare timeout in the namespace) and WITHOUT implicit conversion to int, which kills the family of bugs comparing error with magic number or adding errors by accident. Include the explicit success case (ok = 0) and reading becomes natural.

The historical problem of error codes was never expressiveness, it was IGNORABILITY: the caller forgets to look at the return and the failure vanishes. The modern answer is the [[nodiscard]] attribute on the function: discarding the return becomes a compiler WARNING, and a warning in a serious project becomes an ERROR on CI (-Werror). Forgetting goes from latent bug to broken build, which is where bugs should die.

Complete it with the non-negotiable cultural rule: NO failure is swallowed in silence. If the conscious decision is to move on, the minimum is logging it; the error path without a trace is the most expensive to debug later.

## std::error_code and the map of boundaries

The standard library has its own infrastructure for codes: std::error_code, a value-category pair carrying errors from different origins (operating system, libraries, yours) in a single type, without allocation and without exception. It is what std::filesystem uses in the overloads with an error_code parameter, the no-throw alternative to each operation. Worth knowing for interop; for domain code, your own small, specific enum class usually communicates better.

The module's complete map, then: exceptions for the exceptional crossing layers; expected for expected failure with a reason, in new APIs; optional for absence; enum class with [[nodiscard]] where the error-code style is the rule (C boundaries, projects without exceptions, hot paths not tolerating unwinding). The four coexist in the same system, each on its own floor.

What coexists with none of them is silent failure. Whatever the vehicle, the review question is the same: "if this fails at 3 a.m., what trace remains?". If the answer is none, the PR is not ready.

# The no-throw contract

noexcept is a verifiable promise: this function does NOT throw. If the promise is broken and an exception tries to leave a noexcept function, the program calls std::terminate on the spot. Notice the design: it is not UB, not an escaping exception; it is immediate and loud termination. The contract is hard on purpose, because whoever depends on it makes irreversible decisions.

The biggest dependent you already know from the move module: vector uses move_if_noexcept on reallocation. Move noexcept, it moves; move without the mark, it COPIES everything to preserve the strong guarantee. That is reason number one to mark: move constructor and move assignment noexcept whenever the implementation allows (and pointer stealing allows: no allocation, no throwing).

The second effect is on generated code: calls to noexcept functions dispense that stretch's unwinding infrastructure, which shrinks the binary and unlocks local optimizations. It is a real gain, but smaller than the vector's; treat it as a bonus, not a motive.

[["Where to mark noexcept","Why"],["Move ctor and move assignment","vector moves on reallocation; otherwise copies"],["swap","Base of assignment and rollback idioms"],["Destructors","Already implicit; throwing from them is terminate"],["Cleanup functions and handlers","They run on error paths; they cannot fail"],["Everything indiscriminately","NO: a contract hard to revert later"]]
noexcept is not an optimization, it is a PROMISE with a death penalty: broken, terminate. Mark it where semantics guarantee it, not where the benchmark asked.

## Where to mark, where to resist

The positive list is short and strong. Move and swap: mark them, it is the case with concrete return (vector, rearranging algorithms). Destructors: already implicitly noexcept since C++11; the practical rule is never letting an exception leave one, because a destructor throwing during unwinding is terminate for sure. Cleanup functions, error handlers, callbacks called on a failure path: mark them, whoever handles errors cannot create another.

The resistance list matters equally. Do NOT go marking a whole public API "because it does not throw today": noexcept is an INTERFACE contract, and removing it tomorrow breaks whoever depended on it (including optimization decisions the compiler made on top of the mark). A function whose implementation may legitimately come to throw (allocates, does I/O, calls third-party code) stays unmarked, honestly.

Close with the policing tool: static_assert with is_nothrow_move_constructible on the types depending on cheap move. One line per class, and the promise stops being oral tradition to become a contract the build enforces.

# The contract with the compiler

assert(condition) is EXECUTABLE documentation: it declares a precondition or invariant ("this vector never arrives empty here") and crashes the program at the exact point the premise lied. In release, with NDEBUG defined, asserts vanish completely, zero cost. That duality defines the use: assert is for PROGRAMMING bugs (internal contract violations), never for expected runtime errors (user input, missing file), which stay with the rest of the module's types, active also in release.

The compile-time cousin is static_assert, which verifies properties of types and constants in the build (you saw it locking the move's noexcept). Between the two, a good base covers contracts in both times: what can be proven in the build, static_assert; what only exists in execution, assert.

And asserts have a bigger role than they seem: they mark the border of UNDEFINED BEHAVIOR, the subject closing the module and one C++ forces you to truly understand.

UB is not 'sometimes works': it is the compiler optimizing on top of the promise that it NEVER happens. Working in the test is the disguise, not the acquittal.

## UB: the clause you signed without reading

Undefined behavior is C++'s central contract: the language promises maximum performance in exchange for you NEVER doing certain things (signed int overflow, out-of-bounds access, using a freed pointer, data races). About violating code, the standard promises NOTHING: not a crash, not a message, not consistency between builds.

The point separating those who understand from those who memorize: the compiler OPTIMIZES assuming UB does not happen. It deletes checks that "cannot" be true, reorders accesses, removes entire loops. That is why the program with UB "works" in debug and breaks in optimized release, or works on this compiler version and not the next. The test that passed does not prove absence of UB; it proves that TODAY the roulette stopped on a good number.

The 2026 defense is an industry standard: SANITIZERS on CI. ASan and UBSan instrument the test binary and turn silent UB into a loud error with a stack trace, at a cost that runs in any pipeline. Green tests with sanitizers on: that is the operational definition of "no known UB", and the tenth item of the checklist closing the trail in the final project.

# Reading the crime scene

The project closing the trail is a guided reading: you will take a Buffer class written in the classes-with-C style of twenty years ago and modernize it lesson by lesson, applying everything the previous modules built. The code below is real in the worst sense: it compiles, "works" on the happy path, and carries a complete collection of management crimes.

Before moving to the next block, read the class and list the problems yourself. It is the most honest review exercise there is: no diff, no PR description, only the code and your criteria. Look for ownership, for copying, for const, for the error paths.

The canonical list, to check against yours: the empty destructor leaves the new[] without delete[] (leak on EVERY instance); copiarDe copies the POINTER, not the data (shallow copy: two objects owning the same block); the public members let any code swap the pointer or the size and break the invariant; there is not ONE const in the class; and the compiler-generated copy (constructor and assignment) is shallow too, with the same two owners.

[["Crime in the code","Concrete consequence"],["new[] without delete[] in the destructor","A leak on every Buffer created"],["copiarDe copies the pointer","Two owners of the same block; chaos waiting"],["Generated copy is shallow too","Buffer b2 = b1 duplicates ownership"],["Public members","Any code breaks the invariant"],["No const in the class","Reading and writing indistinguishable in the API"]]
Legacy code is not old code: it is code whose contracts live in the head of someone who already left the company. Modernizing is bringing the contracts into the code.

## Why it 'works', and the attack plan

The uncomfortable question: how did such code survive twenty years? Because its crimes are SILENT. The leak only takes down long-lived processes; the shallow copy only explodes when someone copies AND both objects are truly used; and since the destructor is empty, not even a double free denounces it (two correct destructors would have turned the shallow copy into an immediate crash, which is the bug's way of calling for help). The legacy stands on an equilibrium of defects hiding each other, and that is why fixing ONE crime at a time can UNCAP another: fixing the destructor without touching the shallow copy converts a leak into a double free.

That observation defines the next lessons' method: changes in layers, each leaving the class in a coherent state. Lesson 2: RAII on storage, destructor and copy correct at once (rule of zero). Lesson 3: explicit move with noexcept, and the cost in vector<Buffer> conceptually measured. Lesson 4: the external API, with const, span, and typed errors. Lesson 5: the checklist you take to your reviews.

# The destructor that disappears

The modernization's first layer attacks the root of all crimes: raw storage. The move is not writing the missing delete[]; it is making the resource live in an RAII MEMBER, and letting the rule of zero work.

With std::vector<char> as storage, the transformation is brutal: the destructor disappears (the vector releases), the copy becomes DEEP for free (copying the Buffer copies the block), move comes along and noexcept, and the pointer-size invariant stops existing as a problem, because the vector carries both tied together. The class shrinks and every removed line was a line that could have a bug.

The alternative when resizing is not part of the contract: std::unique_ptr<char[]> plus a std::size_t. You gain a smaller object (the vector keeps three pointers; the unique_ptr, one) and the structural guarantee that nobody "grows" the buffer by accident. You pay with work: the copy disappears (unique_ptr does not copy; the compiler suppresses the class's copy) and, if copy makes sense, you write it deep, by hand, as in the next lesson.

The refactor's best line is the one you erase: every special function the compiler now generates is a function nobody maintains wrong anymore.

## Choosing between A and B with criteria

Which option does the project follow? It depends on the CONTRACT the Buffer promises, and it is an honest design decision in both directions. If the buffer is a work block that grows, shrinks, and serves as assembly area, the vector is unbeatable: all the mechanics ready, tested, with the names the ecosystem knows. If the buffer represents a resource FIXED in size by construction (an image frame, a packet of negotiated size), the unique_ptr version documents that rigidity in the type itself: there is no resize for someone to call by mistake.

Notice the reasoning pattern, because it is the trail's real product: the storage choice left "whatever" for a sentence with criteria (size contract, object cost, who needs to copy). It is exactly the sentence your modernization PR's description must contain.

For the project, we follow option B, unique_ptr plus size: it leaves copy and move EXPLICIT, which is what the next lesson needs to teach. In a real system, option A would be the default recommendation, and you already know how to defend both.

# Explicit move, conscious copy

With unique_ptr as storage, the class's move almost writes itself: Buffer(Buffer&&) noexcept = default works, because unique_ptr knows how to move (the pointer changes owner and the source is left null). The =default is the preferred form: less of your code, standard semantics, and the explicit noexcept documents and locks the contract vector demands.

But there is a grown-up detail in =default: it moves EACH member, and moving a std::size_t is... copying it. After the move, the source is left with dados_ null and tam_ INTACT: a state violating the informal invariant "tam_ describes dados_". Since a moved object is valid-but-unspecified, that is acceptable under the language's contract; but if YOUR invariant demands coherence (for example, tamanho() is callable in any state), write the move by hand zeroing the source's tam_, as in the example. It is a contract decision, and now you have the vocabulary to make it consciously.

The copy, suppressed by unique_ptr, returns by hand and DEEP: it allocates a new block and copies the bytes. Explicit cost, visible in the signature, exactly where a review reader will look.

The difference between a vector<Buffer> that flies and one that crawls is one word in the move's signature. The compiler does not warn which you wrote; the profiler does.

## Measuring the difference, if only mentally

You need no benchmark to REASON about the gain; you need the napkin math the previous modules gave you. A vector<Buffer> with proper reserve and push_back of temporaries: with noexcept move, every insertion is a pointer swap, constant and tiny cost. Without move (or with move without noexcept, which for vector is the same on reallocation), every growth of the vector recopies ALL blocks already inserted: with 100 buffers of 1 MB, a single reallocation moves hundreds of megabytes through memory.

The conceptual experiment worth running in your environment: fill a vector<Buffer> with and without noexcept on the move, measure with a profiler or even a clock, and check the prediction. More important than the number is the habit: static_assert(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<Buffer>) enters the project's header so nobody regresses that contract without breaking the build.

Modernization's state after this lesson: correct destructor, explicit deep copy, coherent noexcept move. What is missing is the SHELL: the API the outside world uses, with const, views, and typed errors. It is the last layer, in the next lesson.

Third, TYPED ERRORS on creation that can fail: the deArquivo factory returns std::expected<Buffer, ErroBuffer>. A missing file is not exceptional in its domain; it is a named result, in the return, with [[nodiscard]] guaranteeing nobody pretends not to have seen it.

The good API is the one making the error AWKWARD to write: size tied to the pointer, const on what reads, typed reason on what fails. The rest is the compiler collecting.

## span, the same discipline as string_view

std::span (C++20) deserves its own paragraph because it closes an old C wound: the (pointer, size) pair traveling SEPARATE through signatures, with every function hoping to receive the two coherent. The span ties them into a single object, light (two registers), non-owning, with the const variant documenting immutability. It is for the contiguous block what string_view is for text, and it carries the SAME lifetime rule: the window does not extend the owner's life; a span stored beyond the Buffer's scope is dangling waiting for a read.

Notice also the factory's design: the constructor became private and public creation goes through deArquivo, which validates BEFORE constructing. A constructed object is a valid object; the "half-built, check later" state died with the legacy's old API.

The class is ready: RAII on storage, honest move, conscious copy, const on reading, views at the boundary, typed error on creation. From the original file, the intent remains. The last lesson turns the whole journey into a checklist that fits your next review.

# The modern C++ checklist for code review

The Buffer's journey condensed the whole trail: value and const in module 1, RAII and ownership in 2, move in 3, the STL's costs in 5, typed errors in 6, and the generic boundary that module 4's templates sustain underneath the library. What stays for the routine is a CHECKLIST: ten questions you run on any C++ PR, yours or others', in the order the problems usually hurt.

Use it as a reading ruler, not bureaucracy. On a small PR, the ten items take five minutes; on a PR tripping on three of them, you just saved a production incident. And notice ALL items are verifiable by reading signature and structure, running nothing: it is contract review, the cheapest there is.

The table below is the trail's final artifact. Copy it to your review template, adjust the vocabulary to your team, and treat every exception to an item as something deserving a justification sentence in the PR description.

[["Checklist item","What to check in review"],["1. Clear ownership","The signature says who owns; no naked new/delete"],["2. Rule of zero","RAII members before any manual special function"],["3. const by default","Reading methods and parameters marked"],["4. Right passing","const T& for expensive; value for cheap or ownership"],["5. Honest move","Move noexcept where there is a resource; no std::move in return"],["6. Return by value","No output parameter; elision works"],["7. vector first","Another container only with the named access pattern"],["8. Typed errors","optional, expected, or enum [[nodiscard]]; nothing mute"],["9. Views with a live owner","string_view and span never outlive the origin"],["10. UB under watch","asserts on preconditions; sanitizers green on CI"]]
A checklist does not replace thinking: it compresses experience. The ten items fit on a card; the criteria to apply them, exception by exception, is what this trail trained.

## Where to point that criteria now

The fastest way to consolidate what you built here is reviewing your OWN old code with the checklist in hand. Pick a class you wrote before the trail and do to it what we did with the Buffer: list the crimes, attack in layers, write the reason for each choice. The second recommended reading is the standard library itself: notice how the signatures of vector, string_view, and expected practice exactly the contracts you learned to demand.

About the language's future, keep the posture the whole trail practiced: in 2026, C++20 is the common base, C++23 already delivers expected and println on the three major compilers, and C++26 comes with contracts and reflection on the horizon. New tools will keep arriving; the PILLARS you took from here (value semantics, explicit ownership, RAII, conscious cost, typed error) have been stable for a decade and remain what separates code that survives from code that haunts.

The rest is deliberate practice: one review a day with this trail's ruler is worth more than any summary.
